claims.text: Argon–nitrogen annealing combined with cyclic tensile straining refines the microstructure of rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The refined microstructure has a more uniform and optimized grain- and phase-boundary geometry.
Microstructural refinement enhances magnetic entropy change at low applied fields.
The refined boundary geometry preserves efficient thermal pathways.
The refined microstructure maintains low hysteresis and mechanical stability.
The untreated alloy has a broad grain-size distribution and relatively unoptimized phase-boundary characteristics.
The treatment produces controlled grain-boundary geometry and phase segregation.
The treatment induces nanoscale ordering.
The treatment homogenizes the distribution of phase boundaries.
Nanoscale ordering and homogenized phase boundaries enable a more uniform magnetic phase transition.
A more uniform magnetic phase transition produces a stronger low-field magnetocaloric response.
Optimized boundary geometry supports rapid heat transport.
Optimized boundary geometry minimizes internal friction, thereby reducing hysteresis.
Reduced internal friction and optimized boundary geometry maintain mechanical stability during repeated cycling.
Treated samples will show a statistically significant increase in low-field magnetocaloric response relative to untreated samples.
Treated samples will have reduced magnetic hysteresis relative to untreated samples.
Treated samples will have improved mechanical durability under cyclic use relative to untreated samples.
The hypothesis is expected to hold near the magnetic transition for rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys whose microstructures are amenable to post-processing refinement.
The hypothesis is limited to treatment regimes that do not overly compromise bulk material properties.
The quantitative dependence of microstructural refinement on treatment duration, temperature, and strain amplitude is not yet established.
